analysis.one_liner: Bars homebuilders from forcing new-home buyers into mandatory arbitration agreements.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop companies that build new houses from making buyers sign a binding arbitration agreement as a condition of buying a home, and from burying arbitration clauses inside the main purchase contract. If an arbitration clause were included, it would have to be a separate document stating plainly that the buyer is giving up the right to go to court, and the buyer would get a say in picking the arbitrator. Violations would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission as unfair and deceptive practices, and a violating arbitration agreement would be void.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying newly built homes. Construction defects and contract disputes are common in new construction, and mandatory arbitration clauses strip buyers of their day in court, often in a private process chosen and paid for by the builder. The bill would have let buyers keep the right to sue and forced any arbitration agreement to be a separate, clearly labeled choice made after a dispute arises.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits builders from requiring a purchaser to agree to mandatory arbitration before signing a home purchase contract, preserving the buyer's access to the courts.
It requires any arbitration agreement to be a separate document that contains only arbitration language and carries the warning that agreeing to arbitration means giving up the right to go to court.
It bars builders from naming the arbitrator in advance and requires a procedure giving the buyer a role in choosing the arbitrator after a dispute actually arises.
Violations would be treated as unfair and deceptive acts under the Federal Trade Commission Act, and the offending arbitration agreement would have no force or effect.

analysis.who_pays: Homebuilding companies, which would lose a contractual tool that limits their exposure to class-action lawsuits and jury trials over construction defects, and the arbitration industry, which would lose a stream of builder-drafted cases. Some enforcement burden would fall on the FTC.

drawbacks.text: Builders could argue that arbitration resolves construction disputes faster and more cheaply than litigation, and that some of those savings are passed on to buyers in the home price.

The bill does not ban arbitration outright; a buyer could still sign a properly separated arbitration agreement, so the practical protection depends on whether the buyer reads and understands the separate document.
FTC enforcement action-by-action may deter violations but does not give individual buyers a direct remedy if an illegal clause slips into their contract.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to homebuyers is real: a purchase contract with a hidden arbitration clause means losing the right to sue over a defective home, often before ever meeting a lawyer. The costs to builders are modest by design, since the bill allows voluntary arbitration as a separate agreement and targets only coercive practices. The main weakness is enforcement: the FTC would have to police contracts nationwide, and a buyer who signs an illegal clause has to rely on the agency rather than on their own lawsuit. On balance the bill was a narrow, well-targeted consumer protection whose costs fell on a concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and sent to a subcommittee, and neither chamber ever took it up before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles A. Gonzalez of Texas introduced the bill in the House on March 14, 2007.
It was referred to the Financial Services Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.
It never received a committee markup, a floor vote in the House, or any consideration in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Homebuilders keep the ability to write mandatory arbitration clauses into new-home purchase contracts, and arbitration providers keep that business. Homebuyers gained nothing; they remained free to be required to sign away their day in court as a condition of buying a house.

for.name: Rep. Charles A. Gonzalez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Homebuyers Protection Act and remained its sole sponsor.

for.name: 2 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the primary committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill out; it sat in committee and then in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the second committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup or floor consideration followed.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only that the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats and that no committee or floor votes were ever held, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Builders would lose the ability to require buyers to arbitrate construction-defect and contract disputes, which currently shifts disputes into a private forum builders help select and shields them from jury trials and class actions. Buyers benefit directly from what builders give up.

Mandatory arbitration clauses in new-home contracts are a source of business for arbitration firms and arbitrators; the bill would shrink that stream of cases and bar builders from pre-naming the arbitrator.
